title: Lamentations 5:1–18
context: Lamentations 5 is the community’s prayer. It has twenty-two verses, matching the number of Hebrew letters, but it is not arranged as an alphabetic acrostic like chapters 1–4. In 5:1–18 the people ask the LORD to remember and see their disgrace. Their inheritance has gone to strangers, they are like orphans and widows, they must pay for water and wood, and they have sought bread from Egypt and Assyria. They say that their fathers sinned and they bear their iniquities, and later they confess, “Woe to us, for we have sinned!” (5:16). They describe servants ruling over them, danger in seeking bread, burning famine, the violation of women in Zion and Judah (5:11), princes hanged, elders dishonored, young men and children forced into hard labor, and joy turned into mourning. The prayer ends this section with Mount Zion lying desolate, with foxes walking on it. Both traditions read the prayer as an honest cry of grief and confession. Jeremiah 31:29–30 and Ezekiel 18 also address the relation between the fathers’ sins and the children’s.

verses.text: Remember, LORD, what has come on us. Look, and see our reproach.
verses.arminianNotes: The community asks the LORD to remember what has come on them and to look and see their disgrace. Arminian readers see a prayer that appeals to God’s attention and compassion, trusting that he will hear.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the prayer as grounded in God’s covenant faithfulness. Both traditions read the opening as a model of honest prayer in suffering, bringing the people’s need before the LORD.

verses.text: Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers, our houses to aliens.
verses.arminianNotes: The community says their inheritance has gone to strangers and their houses to foreigners. Arminians see the loss of the land promised to their ancestors, which was a sign of God’s covenant blessing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the loss of the inheritance as a covenant judgment (compare Deuteronomy 28:30). Both traditions read the verse as the people’s lament over losing what God had given.

verses.text: We are orphans and fatherless. Our mothers are as widows.
verses.arminianNotes: The community says they are orphans and fatherless, and their mothers are like widows. Arminian readers see the deep vulnerability of the people, who have lost their protectors and their place.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image as describing the breakdown of family and community. Both traditions note that the law called God’s people to care for orphans and widows (Deuteronomy 10:18), which makes their present state all the more painful.

verses.text: We must pay for water to drink. Our wood is sold to us.
verses.arminianNotes: The community says they must pay for water to drink and buy their own wood. Arminians see the humiliation of a people forced to buy what was once freely theirs in their own land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as showing the hardship of life under foreign rule. Both traditions read it as part of the people’s detailed lament, bringing even ordinary needs before God.

verses.text: Our pursuers are on our necks. We are weary, and have no rest.
verses.arminianNotes: The community says their pursuers are on their necks, and they are weary with no rest. Arminian readers see the oppression and exhaustion of a conquered people, who find no relief.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the lack of rest as the opposite of the rest God once promised in the land (compare Deuteronomy 12:9–10). Both traditions read the verse with compassion for the people’s suffering.

verses.text: We have given our hands to the Egyptians, and to the Assyrians, to be satisfied with bread.
verses.arminianNotes: The community says they gave their hands to Egypt and Assyria to be satisfied with bread. Arminians see the people’s past reliance on foreign powers, which the prophets condemned as a failure to trust God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as confessing misplaced trust. Both traditions note that giving the hand may mean making a treaty or submitting, and they hold the exact sense open while agreeing on its main point.

verses.text: Our fathers sinned, and are no more. We have borne their iniquities.
verses.arminianNotes: The community says their fathers sinned and are no more, and they bear their iniquities. Arminian readers see the people feeling the weight of past generations’ sins, while noting that verse 16 adds their own confession.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as describing the corporate effects of sin across generations. Both traditions note that Jeremiah 31:29–30 and Ezekiel 18 address this question, and they read the verse together with verse 16 rather than as a denial of personal guilt.

verses.text: Servants rule over us. There is no one to deliver us out of their hand.
verses.arminianNotes: The community says servants rule over them, and no one delivers them from their hand. Arminians see the reversal of order, as those of low status now have power over God’s people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as describing life under foreign officials. Both traditions read it as part of the people’s lament over their humiliation and helplessness.

verses.text: We get our bread at the peril of our lives, because of the sword in the wilderness.
verses.arminianNotes: The community says they get bread at the risk of their lives because of the sword in the wilderness. Arminian readers see the danger of ordinary life in a ruined land, where even finding food is a life-threatening task.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as describing the continuing effects of judgment. Both traditions read it as a sober picture of the people’s suffering after the city’s fall.

verses.text: Our skin is black like an oven, because of the burning heat of famine.
verses.arminianNotes: The community says their skin is hot like an oven from the burning heat of famine. Arminians see the physical suffering of hunger, which the people bring honestly before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image as describing the effects of famine on the body. Both traditions read the verse with compassion, as part of the people’s honest lament.

verses.text: They ravished the women in Zion, the virgins in the cities of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: The community says women were violated in Zion and virgins in the cities of Judah. Arminian readers receive this verse with grief, naming the cruelty done to the vulnerable without elaboration, and they see God’s people bringing even this sorrow to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse soberly, as a witness to the evil of the conquerors and the suffering of the innocent. Both traditions hold the violence as wrong, and they read the verse as lament and a cry for God’s justice.

verses.text: Princes were hanged up by their hands. The faces of elders were not honored.
verses.arminianNotes: The community says princes were hanged by their hands and elders were not honored. Arminians see the humiliation and cruel treatment of the people’s leaders under the conquerors.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as describing the breakdown of honor and authority. Both traditions note that the details may refer to execution or to public display, and they read the verse soberly.

verses.text: The young men carry millstones. The children stumbled under loads of wood.
verses.arminianNotes: The community says young men carry millstones and children stumble under loads of wood. Arminian readers see forced labor laid on the young, who were made to do work meant for animals or servants.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as describing the oppression of a conquered people. Both traditions read it with compassion, as part of the people’s lament over the suffering of their youth.

verses.text: The elders have ceased from the gate, and the young men from their music.
verses.arminianNotes: The community says the elders have left the gate and the young men their music. Arminians see the loss of both community leadership and joyful celebration, which marked the people’s life before the fall.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the gate as the place of judgment and counsel. Both traditions read the verse as describing the collapse of ordinary community life under judgment.

verses.text: The joy of our heart has ceased. Our dance is turned into mourning.
verses.arminianNotes: The community says the joy of their heart has ceased and their dancing has turned to mourning. Arminian readers see the deep sorrow that has replaced the people’s former celebrations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the reversal of joy as a sign of judgment. Both traditions note that Psalm 30:11 speaks of the opposite change, mourning turned into dancing, and they read this verse as the people’s present reality.

verses.text: The crown has fallen from our head. Woe to us, for we have sinned!
verses.arminianNotes: The community says the crown has fallen from their head and confesses, “Woe to us, for we have sinned!” Arminians see a clear confession of guilt, which is essential for true repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the confession as an acknowledgment that the judgment was deserved. Both traditions hold this as shared ground about confession, and they note that it balances verse 7’s reference to the fathers’ sins.

verses.text: For this our heart is faint. For these things our eyes are dim:
verses.arminianNotes: The community says their hearts are faint and their eyes are dim because of these things. Arminian readers see the people’s grief and exhaustion, which they bring honestly to God in prayer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as introducing the reason in verse 18. Both traditions see the dim eyes as recalling the dimmed gold of 4:1, and they read the verse as part of the people’s lament.

verses.text: for the mountain of Zion, which is desolate. The foxes walk on it.
verses.arminianNotes: The community says their grief is for Mount Zion, which is desolate, with foxes walking on it. Arminians see the ruin of the holy mountain as the deepest sorrow, since it was the place of God’s presence among his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image of foxes as showing the complete desolation of Zion. Both traditions read the verse as the climax of the people’s lament before they turn to God’s eternal reign.
